title: Pune Restaurant Bills to Rise 10-15% Before Diwali as Costs Surge
excerpt: Maharashtra restaurants will revise menus in the next eight to 10 days as LPG, vegetables, dairy, wages and rent climb — some dishes could rise 18%.
body:
• Pune and Maharashtra restaurants plan menu price rises of 10-15% in the next eight to 10 days, completing revisions before Diwali, with some dishes up to 18% costlier.
  • Drivers cited are commercial LPG up sharply, plus vegetables, dairy, edible oils, poultry, wages, rentals and excise fees on alcohol.
  • On a Rs 1,000 family bill, a 10-15% rise means Rs 100-150 more before tax; smaller eateries face extra pressure if water restrictions force tanker purchases.
  • Not every operator is raising prices the same way — some Mumbai groups are cutting or holding selective prices, so check the new menu dish by dish.

A festive-season bill that arrives before Diwali

Dining out in Pune is about to get more expensive, and the timing is deliberate. Restaurants across Maharashtra are preparing menu revisions of 10% to 15% over the next eight to 10 days, with most establishments expected to finalise new pricing ahead of Diwali, according to Mirror Now reporting on industry associations. A separate Pune-focused report, summarising Punekar News via Urban Acres, puts the same range for Pune and warns some individual dishes could rise by as much as 18%.

The increase is not a festive surcharge. Operators say it is a pass-through of costs they have absorbed for months — and that the old rhythm of revising menus once every four to seven months no longer works. Some owners now review prices monthly.

What is pushing costs up

Vijay K. Shetty, president of the Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association (AHAR), told reporters commercial LPG cylinder prices have surged, while labour, commercial rent and dairy costs have also moved up sharply. The Pune reporting lists the same stack: commercial LPG, vegetables, dairy products, wages and rentals. Mirror Now adds dairy, edible oils, poultry and fresh produce inflation to the list.

Beyond the kitchen, two slower pressures are building. Amit Kumar Sharma, an executive committee member of the Hotel and Restaurant Association of Western India (HRAWI), pointed to an uneven monsoon and drought concerns in Maharashtra disrupting farm supply chains and lifting vegetable and fruit prices. For smaller eateries, a second risk follows: if municipal water is restricted, they may have to buy from private tankers, adding a daily operating cost that larger hotels can absorb more easily.

Saili Jahagirdar, Pune chapter head of the National Restaurant Association of India (NRAI), said restaurants are also evaluating higher prices for alcoholic beverages after revisions in excise fees — so the drinks bill may rise alongside food.

Not a uniform hike — and not everyone agrees

The headline range hides variation. Increases will differ by dish, cuisine and rent burden, and the Pune report itself notes it did not identify how many restaurants have finalised revisions or a single city-wide announcement covering all of them. In Mumbai, restaurateurs interviewed by Curly Tales described the same cost pressures — Rahul Kotyan of Paashh in Bandra cited net margins of just 3-6% — but split on the response. Some favoured selective, dish-wise revisions and menu engineering before passing costs on; DU Hospitality said it would cut prices by 10-15% across several of its Mumbai restaurants ahead of the festive season to keep premium dining accessible.

"Changes are implemented only after a careful evaluation of market conditions and competition."

— Amit Kumar Sharma, HRAWI executive committee member, via Mirror Now

That split matters for diners. A thali or dosa-idli staple, where customers expect everyday prices to hold, faces different pressure from a special-occasion dish — a point South Indian operators in Mumbai made explicitly about keeping staples affordable.

What this means for you

For families in Pune planning Diwali meals out, budget the arithmetic now: a Rs 2,000 dinner becomes roughly Rs 2,200 to Rs 2,300 at a 10-15% revision, before any alcohol excise pass-through. For diaspora readers visiting home for the festival, the same maths applies to the large family dinners that anchor a trip — the per-head cost, not just the menu headline, is what moves.

What to watch next is whether further revisions follow. Industry members warned that if drought tightens vegetable supply further, another round is possible. For now, the first round is set to land within days — check the printed menu price, not last month's memory of it, when the bill arrives.
